title: Ads
subtitle: 39 ad angles and formats, grouped by when to reach for them. Pick 6–8, not all 39.
startHere: If you have almost no customers yet, lead with problem, contrast, and founder demo formats: 5, 6, 10, 12, 23, 27, 32, 35, 39.
If you have even 5–10 real buyers, add proof wrappers: 28, 29, 34. Save review-site and urgency formats until the proof is real.
shipAdvice: Ship 6–8 ads, not 39. Same angle, different wrapper. Kill anything that does not hold attention past 3 seconds.

categories.title: News, urgency, and pattern breaks
categories.blurb: Only as strong as the real event behind them. Don't invent news or scarcity — it trains people to ignore you.

ads.name: Breaking news
ads.frame: Lower-third or news-desk look: “New: [specific claim].” Early stage: founder at a desk, bold caption, one concrete fact.
ads.why: Works when you have a real launch, a study, or a category shift. Do not invent a news event.

ads.name: Low-stock alert
ads.frame: Red banner, units left, countdown.
ads.why: Only if inventory is actually limited. Fake scarcity trains people to ignore you and can get the ad rejected.

ads.name: We're sorry
ads.frame: Apology open: “Sorry we sold out” or “Sorry this took so long to launch.” Useful at restock or after a waitlist.
ads.why: Needs a real event behind it.

ads.name: Warning
ads.frame: Yellow/black label, “Warning: if you do X, this happens.” Good for a costly mistake your product prevents.
ads.why: Keep the claim specific and supportable.

ads.name: Emergency
ads.frame: “Case of emergency” checklist energy.
ads.why: Best for acute problems (stain, deadline, outage, flare-up), weak for lifestyle brands.

categories.title: Proof wrappers
categories.blurb: Only pull real reviews, real screenshots, real customers. Thin or faked proof looks staged and costs trust.

ads.name: Trustpilot reviews
ads.frame: Stars and review cards on screen.
ads.why: Only pull real reviews. Early brands usually do not have enough volume; a thin 4.9 from 3 reviews looks staged.

ads.name: Zero stars
ads.frame: Opens on a 1-star complaint about the old way, then shows your fix.
ads.why: The bad review is about the category or a competitor behavior, not a fake review of you.

ads.name: Reddit style
ads.frame: Dark-mode post, title, upvotes, a comment thread. Write it in the subreddit's voice.
ads.why: Do not fake a real thread. “Posted in r/ADHD” energy, original copy.

ads.name: Email screenshot
ads.frame: Inbox mock with a subject line like “this actually worked.”
ads.why: Use a real customer email with permission, or label it as a reconstruction.

ads.name: Text message
ads.frame: iMessage bubbles: friend recommends the product.
ads.why: Highest trust when it is a real screenshot. Scripted versions still work if the wording is messy, not ad-copy.

ads.name: Testimonial
ads.frame: Face to camera, specific result, timeframe, and what failed before. One named customer beats a montage.
ads.why: Early stage: offer the product free for an honest 20-second clip.

categories.title: Interface mimics
categories.blurb: Cheap to shoot, native to the feed. Best default wrapper for a brand nobody knows yet.

ads.name: iPhone Notes
ads.frame: Yellow notes app, a short list or confession typed out.
ads.why: Cheap and native. Use for “what I stopped doing” or “3 things I wish I knew.”

ads.name: Google search
ads.frame: Search bar types the problem, results appear, your answer is the click.
ads.why: Strong when people already search the pain (“why does my focus crash at 3pm”).

ads.name: Instagram story
ads.frame: Polls, question stickers, handwritten text, casual vertical.
ads.why: Feels organic. Founder can shoot this in one take.

ads.name: Native
ads.frame: Looks like a normal post in the feed: no logo open, no packshot in frame one, caption does the selling.
ads.why: Best default for a new brand. The product enters after the hook.

categories.title: Problem and contrast
categories.blurb: The most reliable structures on this list. Name the real alternative, show the mess before the logo.

ads.name: Us vs them
ads.frame: Split screen: old habit vs your product.
ads.why: Name the alternative people already use (another app, coffee, willpower), not a straw man.

ads.name: Myth vs fact
ads.frame: Two lines. Myth in red, fact in plain type.
ads.why: Good for a category full of bad advice. One myth per ad.

ads.name: Don't be an idiot
ads.frame: Blunt callout of a common mistake.
ads.why: Tone has to match the audience. Fine for builders and operators, wrong for anxious or clinical categories.

ads.name: Problem vs solution
ads.frame: Left side is the mess, right side is the outcome, product is the bridge.
ads.why: The most reliable structure on this list. Show the problem before the logo.

ads.name: You can avoid
ads.frame: “You can avoid [cost] if you stop [behavior].”
ads.why: Future-pace the pain, then one action.

ads.name: Problems
ads.frame: Rapid list of pains, each crossed out or stacked. End on the one problem you actually solve.
ads.why: Do not claim the whole list.

ads.name: Don't buy this
ads.frame: Reverse psychology: “Don’t buy this if you already [have the outcome].”
ads.why: Filters the wrong buyer and raises curiosity. Needs a real reason someone should not buy.

ads.name: New vs old
ads.frame: Before/after of the method, not just the result.
ads.why: “Old way: 4 apps and a spreadsheet. New way: one check-in.”

categories.title: Lists and education
categories.blurb: Teach something real. A self-diagnosis hook or a true mechanism earns attention even from people who never buy.

ads.name: Tier list
ads.frame: S-to-F ranking of options in the category, your product placed with a reason.
ads.why: Works once you can defend the ranking. Arrogant if you have no track record.

ads.name: X signs
ads.frame: “5 signs your [system] is broken.” Self-diagnosis hook.
ads.why: Viewer counts how many apply, then you offer the fix.

ads.name: Reasons why
ads.frame: Numbered reasons, one per cut. Easy to shoot: founder, whiteboard, or text cards.
ads.why: Lead with the least obvious reason.

ads.name: Hack 101
ads.frame: One tactic, taught fast, product is the shortcut.
ads.why: Best early-stage format if you have a real mechanism. Teach the trick even if they never buy.

ads.name: Stat headline
ads.frame: One number, huge type: “73% of…”
ads.why: Only use a number you can source. Invented stats get skipped and can fail review.

categories.title: Production styles
categories.blurb: Film founder versions of a proven script before paying for AI podcast or claymation versions of an unproven one.

ads.name: Offer
ads.frame: Price, bundle, or guarantee is the visual.
ads.why: Useful after the angle is proven. Cold traffic rarely converts on a discount alone when the brand is unknown.

ads.name: Script
ads.frame: Teleprompter-style read, full script on screen or burned-in captions, founder talking straight.
ads.why: Write the hook in line one. Record 5 hooks, keep one body.

ads.name: Whiteboard
ads.frame: Marker, arrows, before/after diagram.
ads.why: High trust for anything with a mechanism (habit, finance, health, software). Phone on a tripod is enough.

ads.name: AI podcast
ads.frame: Two hosts, waveform, “we tested this” conversation.
ads.why: Pattern interrupt because it does not look like UGC. Keep claims ordinary — a fake expert with medical or financial claims is a review risk.

ads.name: Doodle
ads.frame: Hand-drawn stick figures over a voiceover.
ads.why: Good when the product is abstract. One idea, 15 seconds.

ads.name: Transformation
ads.frame: Before state, turning point, after state.
ads.why: For an early brand, transform the workflow or the week, not the person, unless you have consented footage.

ads.name: Bundle
ads.frame: Everything they get, stacked visually, price anchor at the end.
ads.why: Use when the offer is the advantage. Weak if the product is not understood yet.

ads.name: Side effect
ads.frame: “Side effect of using this: [unexpected good outcome].”
ads.why: Soft curiosity hook. The side effect has to be true.

ads.name: Claymation
ads.frame: Stop-motion clay look, usually AI-generated. Use it to show a mechanism — the problem as a character, the product as the fix.
ads.why: Stops the scroll because the feed is full of talking heads. Do not make the clay the strategy; put a proven script inside it.

ads.name: Greenscreen
ads.frame: Person in front of a screenshot, article, or product UI, pointing.
ads.why: Fastest way to add proof. Early stage: greenscreen your own app, a calendar, or a customer message.

ads.name: Meme
ads.frame: Existing meme format, your punchline.
ads.why: Good for organic and retargeting. Paid meme ads fatigue in days, so treat them as hooks, not evergreen.

howToRun: Pick one sharp angle. Example: “Your to-do list is why you never start.” Then wrap it four ways: Notes app, problem vs solution, 5 signs, greenscreen demo. Same script spine, different first frame.
Film founder versions before you pay for AI podcast or claymation. Those formats win when the words are already proven — they do not fix a vague product.
On every ad: hook in the first second, product by second 4–6, one claim, one next step. Captions burned in. No logo open.
